explanation: Heating something raises its temperature, but how much depends on the substance. The heat Q (in joules) needed equals the mass m times the specific heat c times the temperature rise delta T. Water has a large c (4186 J/kg/degC), so it heats slowly and resists temperature change — that's why oceans moderate climate. Here a burner pours in heat at a fixed power; with bigger mass or bigger c, the same heat produces a smaller delta T, so the thermometer climbs more slowly.
bullets: Q = m·c·ΔT: more mass or higher specific heat means more joules per degree.
Water's high c (4186 J/kg·°C) makes it a thermal sponge — slow to warm, slow to cool.
At constant heating power P, the temperature rises linearly: ΔT = P·t / (m·c).
